GRU4Rec’s official implementation supports both BPR-max and cross-entropy, recommends roughly 2,048 additional negatives, and reports that logQ correction usually helps cross-entropy. A modest negative pool therefore deserves an ablation before attributing weak Electronics margins to the GRU backbone. Compare larger-pool BPR-max against sampled softmax with identical GRU architecture and training budget. These are experimental hypotheses, not established gains on the pinned benchmark. [Official GRU4Rec](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec)

Sampling correction needs care: RecSys 2025’s *Correcting the LogQ Correction* argues that conventional correction mishandles the positive item, which is always included rather than sampled, and reports improvements from a refined formulation. Its evidence concerns retrieval models, so transfer to GRU4Rec remains unverified. NVIDIA’s sampled-softmax implementation also explicitly masks accidental target–negative matches. For this task, exclude padding and target collisions; any history-based rejection changes the proposal distribution and must be reflected in correction. Hard-negative selection likewise changes sampling probabilities, so avoid blindly applying the original proposal’s logQ. [RecSys 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331), [NVIDIA implementation](https://nvidia-merlin.github.io/Transformers4Rec/stable/_modules/transformers4rec/torch/model/prediction_task.html)

Contrastive complexity is not automatically worthwhile: a WWW 2024 study found some augmentation-only methods matched or exceeded contrastive approaches at lower cost. Prioritize objective/pool-size ablations; then consider a small, jointly trained consistency loss without treating similar users as negatives. Observed training positives can identify collisions, but unobserved items remain uncertain negatives. Keep one GRU model per category and select exclusively by fixed macro validation HR@10. [WWW 2024 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11136)
